issues.legal_issue: Prior compensation judgments concerning other land acquisitions do not conclusively determine the market value or entitlement to compensation in a separate acquisition proceeding.
material_facts: The lower courts relied on judgments and awards concerning land in nearby villages when determining compensation.
The High Court treated those earlier judgments and awards as creating res judicata and barred the acquiring authority's appeals.
The earlier judgments and awards were evidence about comparable land, not final determinations of the same inter-party dispute in the present proceeding.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in applying res judicata. Earlier judgments and awards may be admitted as evidence, but do not by themselves prevent the acquiring authority from disputing the claim or presenting other relevant material; the principle also did not bar the claimants' cross-objections.
issues.legal_principle: Res judicata applies when the same lis between the parties has attained finality on the issues in dispute. It does not ordinarily apply to a pure question of law, a judgment of a court lacking jurisdiction, or a non-speaking judgment. Comparable acquisition judgments and awards have evidentiary value, not automatic preclusive effect. The Court relied on Government of West Bengal v. Tarun K. Roy, State of Maharashtra v. Digambar, State of Bihar v. Ramdeo Yadav, Nathi, Shakuntala Devi, and Ramnik Vallabhdas Madhvani.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The dispute concerns compensation for land acquired by the state.
predicates.earlier_awards_concern_other_acquisition: The earlier compensation judgments or awards concern separate acquisitions, including acquisitions of allegedly similar land.
predicates.earlier_awards_do_not_finally_determine_: The earlier judgments or awards do not finally determine the same dispute between the parties in the present proceeding.

issues.definition: When a compensation proceeding relies on awards from separate acquisitions, those awards may be evidence but do not conclusively bar consideration of the present dispute.

issues.legal_issue: A claim to compensation for minerals in acquired land depends on the claimant's proven rights and the statutory limits on extracting those minerals.
material_facts: The claimants asserted rights in land containing china clay, but the deeds establishing the nature and extent of the predecessor's rights were not before the Court.
The village record stated that a mine found in the future would belong to the Government, but did not establish that china clay existed in the land when the relevant rights were granted.
The applicable rules restricted mineral extraction and required permits, and generally did not authorize commercial extraction for private use under the agricultural-land exception.
The lower courts had assessed compensation for china clay without considering the relevant land and mineral laws or the limitations on mining.
issues.conclusion: The Court did not finally determine the claimants' title to the land or mineral rights. It held that a presumption of ownership of china clay could not be drawn for the grantee merely from the village record, absent proof that the mineral existed at the relevant time or that the right was expressly conveyed. Any mineral compensation must account for the claimant's proven rights and statutory restrictions, and cannot be based on profits from unlawful mining.
issues.legal_principle: Ownership of land may include subsoil rights, but a tenant or sub-tenant does not acquire those rights merely by holding agricultural land; the grant and applicable statutes determine their extent. Section 42(2) of the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887 creates a rebuttable presumption concerning certain interests in land, and Section 4 of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 requires mining operations to be conducted under the prescribed authorization. Sections 14 and 15 of that Act address minor minerals and state rule-making; the Court also considered Rules 5 and 7 of the Punjab Minor Mineral Rules, 1934, Sections 22, 23, 39 and 185 of the Delhi Land Reforms Act, and Article 31A of the Constitution. It relied on Gaon Sabha v. Nathi, State of Punjab v. Vishkarma and Co., Raja Rajinder Chand v. Mst. Sukhi, and authorities on the presumption that subsoil rights are not conveyed without express grant.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding and mineral_rights_claimed and (mineral_title_not_proven or statutory_rules_restrict_extraction)

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The dispute concerns compensation for land acquired by the state.
predicates.mineral_rights_claimed: The claimant seeks compensation for minerals in the acquired land.
predicates.mineral_title_not_proven: The claimant has not established that the relevant mineral right was held or expressly conveyed to the claimant.
predicates.statutory_rules_restrict_extraction: Applicable law limits mineral extraction or requires authorization for the extraction claimed.

issues.definition: Where mineral rights are claimed in an acquisition proceeding, compensation is limited to rights the claimant proves and could lawfully exercise.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant who represents that interest will not be claimed for a period in order to obtain a stay may not later claim interest for that period.
material_facts: The claimants asked the Reference Court to stay proceedings and represented that they would not claim interest on any enhanced compensation during the stay.
The acquiring authority did not object to the stay on those terms, and the Court stayed the proceedings accordingly.
The High Court nevertheless allowed interest for the period covered by the stay.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in allowing interest for the period of the stay; the claimants could not claim interest for that period after obtaining the stay on their representation.
issues.legal_principle: Interest under Section 28 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 is discretionary as to whether it is awarded, although the prescribed rate is mandatory when interest is awarded. The Court held that statutory rights may be waived by agreement or conduct where public interest is not involved, and applied the principle that a party may not take advantage of its own representation. It relied on Raghubans Narain Singh v. Uttar Pradesh Government, State of Assam v. Jitendra Kumar Senapati, Krishna Bahadur v. Purna Theatre, Superintendent of Taxes, Dhubri v. Onkarmal Nathmal Trust, and the principle actus curiae neminem gravabit.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The dispute concerns compensation for land acquired by the state.
predicates.claimant_requested_stay: The claimant asked the court to stay the compensation proceedings.
predicates.claimant_waived_interest_during_stay: The claimant represented that interest would not be claimed for the period of the stay, and the stay was granted on that basis.

issues.definition: A claimant who obtains a stay on a representation waiving interest cannot receive interest for the period covered by that representation.

issues.legal_issue: Where the pre-amendment compensation-claim limit applies, compensation awarded by the court cannot exceed the amount claimed in the circumstances specified by that limit.
material_facts: The compensation proceedings arose before the 1984 amendment to the Land Acquisition Act, and the Court held that the earlier version of Section 25 governed.
The claimants had sought specified compensation before the Collector, while the High Court awarded a higher amount.

The High Court found that notice under Sections 9 and 10 had not been served, but the Collector's awards recorded that notice had been issued; the Court held that notice and participation facts required reconsideration.
issues.conclusion: If the unamended Section 25 applies, the High Court could not award compensation above the amount claimed where the applicable statutory conditions were met. The High Court had to reconsider whether notice had been served and whether the relevant statutory conditions applied.
issues.legal_principle: Section 25 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as it stood before the 1984 amendment, imposed limits on the amount the court could award depending on whether the claimant made a claim pursuant to notice, refused or omitted to make a claim, or had sufficient reason for omission. The Court held that this provision was substantive and that the pre-amendment version applied to the proceedings. It relied on Land Acquisition Officer-cum-DSWO v. B.V. Reddy and Sons and Krishi Utpadan Mandi Samiti v. Kanhaiya Lal, and discussed the purpose of Section 9 notice, participation with knowledge of the proceedings, and prejudice.

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding and pre_amendment_claim_limit_applies and compensation_claim_made and notice_or_participation_condition_met

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The dispute concerns compensation for land acquired by the state.
predicates.pre_amendment_claim_limit_applies: The proceeding is governed by the earlier compensation-claim limit rather than a later amendment.
predicates.compensation_claim_made: The claimant stated an amount sought as compensation before the acquiring authority.
predicates.notice_or_participation_condition_met: The claimant received the relevant notice or participated in the proceeding with knowledge sufficient to serve the notice's purpose.

issues.definition: When the earlier claim limit applies and its notice or participation condition is met, an award cannot exceed the claimant's stated compensation claim.

issues.legal_issue: Amending an appeal memorandum does not, by itself, amend the original compensation pleadings, and additional evidence cannot be admitted on the basis of an amendment that was not properly completed.
material_facts: The claimants originally sought specified compensation before the Reference Court and later sought higher compensation by amending their appeal and reference materials.

The High Court allowed amendments and additional evidence without adequately considering the relevant factors, including delay, earlier admissions, the statutory claim limit, and compliance with the time for carrying out amendments.
The amendments were not carried out within the time required by the applicable procedural rule, and no extension of time was granted.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in allowing the amendments and additional evidence on that basis. Amending the appeal memorandum did not amend the original pleadings, and the uncompleted amendments could not support admission of the additional evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Section 53 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 makes the Code of Civil Procedure applicable to proceedings under the Act. Order VI Rule 17 permits amendment of pleadings subject to judicial consideration of relevant factors, including whether the party seeks to withdraw an express admission and whether delay or laches weighs against amendment. Order VI Rule 18 requires an allowed amendment to be carried out within the specified time or, if none is specified, within the prescribed period, unless the court extends time. The Court relied on Modi Spinning & Weaving Mills Co. v. Ladha Ram, Heeralal v. Kalyan Mal, Sangramsinh P. Gaekwad v. Shantadevi P. Gaekwad, and the principles in B.V. Reddy and Sons and Krishi Utpadan Mandi Samiti v. Kanhaiya Lal.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal arising from a land acquisition compensation reference.
predicates.appeal_amendment_does_not_amend_original: The change was made to appeal materials but did not amend the original compensation pleadings.
predicates.amendment_not_completed_within_required_: The party did not carry out an allowed pleading amendment within the required period.
predicates.no_time_extension_granted: The court did not extend the time for carrying out the amendment.

issues.definition: In a compensation appeal, an uncompleted amendment to appeal materials does not change the original pleadings or provide a basis for additional evidence.

issues.legal_issue: Market value must be determined from relevant evidence and the acquired land's characteristics and purpose, rather than by mechanically applying rates for developed residential plots to a large acquisition for another purpose.
material_facts: Approximately 5,000 bighas were acquired for construction of a university, and the land included different categories, hills, and areas bearing minerals.
The High Court based its valuation on rates for developed residential plots and made deductions without adequately explaining the method or considering the other evidence.

The record lacked satisfactory evidence about the cost of filling pits left by mineral extraction, and the land's suitability for construction and its different characteristics had not been properly assessed.
The claimants relied principally on judgments and awards concerning other acquisitions, and the High Court also relied on government circulars concerning residential land.
issues.conclusion: The High Court's valuation method was not justified on the record. The compensation determination had to be reconsidered using relevant evidence and taking account of the acquisition's scale and purpose, differences in land quality and potential, development requirements, mineral rights, and other advantages and disadvantages.
issues.legal_principle: Market value is ordinarily the price a willing purchaser would pay to a willing vendor. Comparable sales and awards may be considered, but comparables must be assessed for proximity, similarity, size, location, and other advantages or disadvantages; development costs and the scale and purpose of acquisition are relevant. Administrative rate registers or circulars without an adequate evidentiary foundation cannot alone establish market value. The Court relied on Land Acquisition Officer v. Nookala Rajamallu, Lila Ghosh v. State of West Bengal, Viluben Jhalejar Contractor v. State of Gujarat, Shaji Kuriakose v. Indian Oil Corporation, Jawajee Nagnatham v. Revenue Divisional Officer, Shakuntalabai v. State of Maharashtra, and other cited market-value decisions.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The dispute concerns compensation for land acquired by the state.
predicates.acquired_land_is_large_or_varied: The acquisition covers a large area or land with materially different categories, characteristics, or potential.
predicates.valuation_relies_on_residential_rates_wi: The valuation uses rates for developed residential plots without adequately assessing the acquired land's differences, purpose, and relevant costs or advantages.

issues.definition: When a large or varied acquisition is valued using residential rates without assessing relevant differences, market value requires reassessment on relevant evidence.

issues.legal_issue: The owner's own purchase of the acquired land is important valuation evidence, and rejecting a request to place that purchase deed before the appellate court solely because it had not earlier been relied upon was erroneous in this case.
material_facts: A claimant had purchased a share of the acquired land before the acquisition notification.
The acquiring authority sought to place a copy of that sale deed before the High Court as additional evidence.
The High Court rejected the application, in part because the authority had not previously sought to rely on the deed.
issues.conclusion: The High Court committed a serious error in rejecting the application on that basis; an owner's purchase of the acquired land is important evidence for determining compensation.
issues.legal_principle: A sale of the acquired land by the owner is relevant evidence of market value and may provide a basis for determining compensation. The Court relied on Shakuntalabai v. State of Maharashtra, which recognizes the significance of an owner's own purchase when assessing the land's value.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal arising from a land acquisition compensation reference.
predicates.owner_purchased_acquired_land_before_acq: The owner acquired the land or an interest in it before the acquisition.
predicates.purchase_deed_is_offered_as_valuation_ev: A party offers the owner's purchase deed as evidence relevant to the land's value.

issues.definition: In a compensation appeal, a deed showing the owner's pre-acquisition purchase of the land is relevant valuation evidence.

issues.legal_issue: A court should not direct payment of all acquisition compensation to one claimant while the competing claimants' entitlement remains unresolved in pending proceedings.
material_facts: Competing parties asserted interests in the acquired land, and their inter se claims were pending in separate proceedings.
The High Court directed payment of the entire compensation to one claimant's family entity despite those pending disputes and without an application by that entity for the direction.
The governing statute preserved the liability of a recipient to pay compensation to the person legally entitled to it.
issues.conclusion: The direction to pay the entire compensation to the family entity was unjustified and was set aside. The entitlement to compensation remained for determination in the pending proceedings, and a recipient found not to be entitled would have to repay the compensation with any interest determined under restitution principles.
issues.legal_principle: Under the third proviso to Section 31(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, a person who receives compensation remains liable to pay it to the person lawfully entitled. Competing title claims must be determined in the appropriate proceedings; receipt of compensation does not finally determine entitlement.

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The dispute concerns compensation for land acquired by the state.
predicates.competing_entitlement_claims_pending: Different claimants assert entitlement to the acquired land or its compensation, and their dispute remains pending.
predicates.compensation_directed_to_one_claimant_be: A court directs payment of the compensation to one claimant before deciding the competing claims.

issues.definition: Where competing entitlement claims remain unresolved, compensation cannot properly be directed exclusively to one claimant before those claims are determined.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may invoke its constitutional power to set aside procedural orders and remit a case to secure complete justice in exceptional circumstances involving mishandled proceedings and substantial public funds.
material_facts: The acquiring authority did not challenge certain orders concerning amendment and additional evidence.
The case involved a large amount of public money and a history of mishandled proceedings and conflicting court orders.
The Supreme Court concluded that the lower courts had not properly considered material legal and evidentiary issues.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to set aside the relevant orders and judgments and remit the matters for fresh consideration.
issues.legal_principle: Article 142 of the Constitution empowers the Supreme Court to make orders necessary to do complete justice between the parties. The Court relied on Deb Narayan Shyam v. State of West Bengal as an example of invoking that power where the state's handling of proceedings had created an anomalous situation.

rule.if: supreme_court_appeal and proceedings_mishandled and substantial_public_funds_involved and existing_orders_prevent_complete_justice

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: The matter is before the Supreme Court on appeal.
predicates.proceedings_mishandled: The proceedings were mishandled, resulting in material procedural or adjudicative errors.
predicates.substantial_public_funds_involved: The dispute involves a substantial amount of public money.
predicates.existing_orders_prevent_complete_justice: The existing orders prevent a fair and complete determination of the dispute.

issues.definition: In an appeal involving mishandled proceedings and substantial public funds, the Supreme Court may set aside existing orders and remit the matter when needed to achieve complete justice.
